summary:
ASTRA Crew Health Monitor is an offline-first astronaut health monitoring prototype designed for long-duration space missions. It combines a digital astronaut body map, real-time biometric dashboard, spaceflight hazard radar, edge-AI triage guidance, mission readiness tracking, and Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking (DTN) data synchronization.

The system is designed to work even when communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable. Health records can be stored locally, prioritized, and forwarded when a communication link returns. The dashboard supports demo scenarios such as EVA exertion, radiation events, CO₂ spikes, and SANS-related eye strain, while also providing a validated API pathway for future medical sensors.

This project addresses the challenge of protecting astronaut health in isolated environments by enabling continuous monitoring, early anomaly awareness, actionable countermeasure guidance, and reliable store-and-forward communication. It is important because astronauts may need immediate, independent health support when Earth-based medical assistance is minutes or hours away.
details:
What does it do?

AstroGuard acts as an intelligent onboard medical copilot. It streams live data from medical hardware—like ECGs, pulse oximeters, and temperature sensors—alongside broader spacecraft telemetry.

Instead of treating every astronaut the same, it compares incoming readings against their personal physiological baseline. If something unusual is detected, it immediately serves up triage guidance and alerts right in the cockpit, cutting through the noise so astronauts can act fast.

Why it’s a game-changer (Benefits)

  • Independent Operations: Fully functional during communication blackouts, solar interference, and deep-space signal delays.
  • Instant Onboard Guidance: Empowers astronauts to manage health issues immediately without waiting for Earth-bound flight surgeons.
  • Stress-Tested UI: Features a clean, distraction-free cockpit interface optimized for high-pressure situations and low-light environments.
  • Smart Alerting: Uses personal health baselines instead of rigid, one-size-fits-all thresholds to drastically reduce unnecessary false alarms.
  • Comprehensive Risk Tracking: Monitors invisible hazards like cosmic radiation, elevated CO₂ levels, isolation fatigue, and bone health risks.
  • Store-and-Forward Sync: Securely logs and stores medical data locally on the spacecraft, automatically syncing organized records back to Earth whenever a connection becomes available.

Mission Impact

AstroGuard is built to elevate safety across ISS operations, future lunar bases, and eventual crewed Mars missions. It bridges the gap between total astronaut self-sufficiency and seamless mission control oversight, ensuring flight surgeons receive clean, organized health histories the moment communication re-establishes.

Under the Hood (Tech Stack)

The current working prototype is powered by a modern, responsive web ecosystem:

  • Frontend & Dashboard: Interactive browser dashboard built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • Backend & Real-Time Sync: Node.js, REST APIs, and Server-Sent Events (SSE) for live biometric updates, backed by lightweight JSON persistence for the prototype.

Future production scaling envisions moving into certified medical hardware, including Kotlin/Android mobile apps, BLE/USB sensors, encrypted local storage with SQLCipher, and cloud-ready synchronization via Supabase/PostgreSQL.

What makes it unique?

What sets AstroGuard apart is its holistic approach to space medicine. It combines several critical layers into a single cohesive experience:

  • An interactive astronaut digital twin
  • A real-time biometric and hazard radar
  • Offline-ready AI triage logic
  • A live mission-readiness scoring system
  • DTN (Delay-Tolerant Networking) store-and-forward communication flows
  • Simulated emergency scenario modes

At its core, the project is built on one golden rule: Never assume Earth is online.

Engineering & Design Considerations

Building medical software for space requires obsessive attention to detail. Every design choice was weighed against real-world spaceflight constraints:

  • Deep-space latency and communication dropouts
  • Astronaut cognitive workload and fatigue under stress
  • Data privacy, local encryption, and medical hardware reliability
  • The fine line between helpful safety alerts and sensor noise / stale data

Note: The current version is a fully functional, controlled demo prototype. Full deployment for real space missions would require certified medical hardware, rigorous clinical trials, secure multi-factor authentication, and mission-approved hardware validation.
